analysis.one_liner: Wipes out the FCC's 2015 net neutrality rules and bars the agency from bringing them back.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted nine Republican senators but never received a committee vote, and it died when the 114th Congress ended with the FCC's net neutrality rules still in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: In February 2015 the FCC reclassified broadband internet as a 'telecommunications service,' which let it enforce net neutrality rules barring internet providers from blocking, throttling, or selling faster lanes to favored websites. This bill would void that entire order and forbid the FCC from reissuing anything like it unless Congress passed a new law specifically allowing it. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband providers — cable, telephone, and wireless companies — gain the most. With the 2015 order voided, they could once again block or slow websites, charge content companies for faster delivery, and operate free of utility-style oversight of rates and practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable, phone, and wireless internet providers

how_it_helps.text: The bill strips the force of law from the FCC's February 26, 2015 order that reclassified broadband internet access as a telecommunications service, eliminating the legal basis for the commission's net neutrality rules.

It goes further than a simple repeal: the FCC could not reissue the rule or adopt any substantially similar one unless Congress enacts a later law specifically authorizing it, so the protections could not be restored by a future commission.
Removing the reclassification frees internet providers from being regulated as common carriers, which backers argued would lift regulatory burdens on network investment.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users pay. Without the rules, their provider could block or slow specific sites and services, and websites could be forced to pay for priority — costs that would show up as higher prices, degraded service, or fewer choices for the public.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently bar the FCC from restoring net neutrality protections on its own, leaving broadband customers without federal rules against blocking, throttling, or paid fast lanes unless Congress acts.

Supporters' core argument — that reclassification would depress broadband investment — was a prediction, not a demonstrated harm, and the bill offered no replacement protections for consumers; it simply removed the FCC's authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a clean transfer of power from the regulator to the broadband industry: providers gain freedom from utility-style rules, and the public gains nothing in exchange — no replacement consumer protections are included. The strongest good-faith case for it rests on the unproven claim that lighter regulation would mean more network investment, while the concrete loss is the elimination of rules against blocking and paid prioritization. Weighed honestly, the costs fall on millions of internet users while the gains flow to a handful of large providers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on February 25, 2016, with seven other Republican senators listed as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
Because the bill never became law, the FCC's 2015 net neutrality order remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers failed to get the net neutrality rules stripped by statute, and internet users kept the FCC's 2015 protections for the time being. The committee's inaction — not a debate or a vote — decided the outcome, so no one had to defend the bill on its merits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet users; the repeal never advanced

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to void the FCC's 2015 broadband reclassification order and bar a substantially similar rule without new congressional authorization.

for.name: 8 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors: Cornyn, Cotton, Cruz, Paul, Rubio, Tillis, Sasse and one more
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none of the Senate's Democrats signed on.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. John Thune (R-SD)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting the bill die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine senators behind the bill were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored it, and it never reached a vote where the full chamber's split could be measured.

industries.industry: Broadband providers (cable, telephone, and wireless internet companies)
industries.note: The bill would void the 2015 order that let the FCC treat broadband providers as common carriers, freeing them to block, slow, or prioritize web traffic for payment and removing rate and practice oversight. Their gain comes directly at the expense of the people who buy their service.

industries.industry: Internet content and edge companies (websites, streaming services, startups)
industries.note: Without net neutrality rules, edge providers could be charged for priority delivery or deprioritized if they don't pay, and the bill barred the FCC from reissuing similar protections. Their interests here track the public's interest in an open internet.
